searches.note: Twenty two searches of a share of forty five, none of them the author's, twenty three left unspent for the run's shared allowance. Five were restricted to a house's or a body's own domain (mouchao.pt three times, esporao.com, cortesdecima.pt, fea.pt), each read as primary through its summary; the rest blocked the author's sources (the houses where the account had to be independent, the CVRA, Agroportal, Observador, Entrée Cuvée, Decanter, Wine Disclosures, Wine Enthusiast and Portugal Get Wine for Cortes de Cima). Writers' own sites that came up were read and never cited. No fetch tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash, no spoken list longer than three in a table line).

The searches went first to the dates the stories turn on (Mouchão's 1901, 1949, 1954 and the return, the Pêra-Manca cession and 1990, the founder's dates, Esporão's 1267, 1973 and 1985, Borba's 1955 and 1964, Cortes de Cima's 1988, 1991 and 1998), then to the making of each flagship against sheets of other vintages, then to the others.

Where a house's own page met an independent account that contradicted it, the house's fact was hedged as its own (the return of 1986, the board of 30 April 1955) and a question keyed on it replaced; where figures differed by vintage they were widened or tied to the vintage (Esporão's oak, Incógnito's making); where a claim rested on nothing read it was cut (the oldest plot, the minty note the house calls its own, the label reading Borba beside Alentejo).

tested: The dates, the house first blocked: 1901 for the winery on Cave Lusa, Salt of Portugal and others among Portugal by Wine, Winexp and Alentasia (one naming John and Rafael Reynolds as its builders), 1904 on Wine Enthusiast; the first bottling of 1949 on the house and Wine Searcher; the Mouchão label of 1954 on the house and a merchant (first sold as Mouchão in 1954); the expropriation after 1974 everywhere; the return 1986 by the house and one account, 1985 by two others among the same pages. The house read afresh on its own domain: 1832, the 1890s, 1901, 1949, 1954 and 1986, the restorers a daughter, her husband and their son.

The family and the grape: an independent account has Thomas Reynolds in Portugal from 1820, in cork from 1838 at Alburquerque in Spain and at Estremoz from 1850; Wine Enthusiast has a later Reynolds, on the phylloxera commission, bring Alicante Bouschet cuttings from Montpellier in the 1880s. The cork trade borne out; the house's around 1832 kept as its own; nobody of the family named, no two sources giving anyone's dates.

The sites and the making, on the house's own sheets: Carrapetos on well drained alluvial loams, planted in 1988 and field grafted in 1989 (2013 sheet), 27 years old at the 2015 harvest, the house's oldest vineyard by its own word; trodden twice a day, four to six days in 2015 and four to seven in other years, malolactic in 5,000 litre tonéis, about three years in them and 24 to 36 months in bottle; 85 per cent Alicante Bouschet and 15 Trincadeira in 2015, as merchants give for 2017. Merchants give two to four years in wood and up to four in bottle, so the figures are tied to the house.

Tonel 3 and 4 on the house's sheet and product page: Carrapetos fruit alone, made only in years of full ripeness, two 5,000 litre casks numbered three and four, three years and two in bottle on the 2013 sheet against at least four and four on the product page.

The questions: the wine question has one right answer and options of one kind; the story question keyed on 1986 rested on the house alone against two accounts of 1985, so it was replaced by one on the cork trade (four trades of the Alentejo or of Portugal, Port removed since the Reynolds patriarch is said to have come to Portugal as a merchant). The house rules: nobody living named, no price, no score, no production (the 2015 bottle count met and not used), no judging superlative, British, no dash.

changed.was: The Reynolds family came to the Alentejo for cork: by the house's own account its forebear moved there around 1832, drawn by the cork trade, and Mouchão, by Casa Branca, was one of the estates where the family worked the cork oaks. There were probably vines there already. In the early 1890s a grandson of the founder of the cork business built the family house and the farm buildings, and in 1901 came the winery, its stone lagares and its layout little changed since. The family is thought to have brought the first Alicante Bouschet vines from France, and that grape, red in its flesh as well as its skin, became the heart of the estate. For decades the wine was sold in bulk; the first bottling came in 1949, and the Mouchão label was born with the harvest of 1954. After the revolution of 1974 the estate was expropriated, and it came back to the family only in 1986, run down, to be restored by a daughter of the family, her husband and a grandson. Mouchão is the Alentejo before modern winemaking: grapes trodden by foot, years in large old wood, and a red that asks for patience.

tested: The founder, the author's sources blocked: Vasco Maria Eugénio de Almeida, born 30 August 1913 and died 11 August 1975, an agronomist trained at the Instituto Superior de Agronomia, second Count of Vilalva, by the Portuguese Wikipedia and the foundation's own page (which has him die a few days before his sixty second birthday, consistent); the foundation of 1963 and its statutes his, by the foundation; he inherited Scala Coeli in 1940, restored it from 1948 to 1960 and opened the way for the Carthusians to return in 1960, and the community left on 31 October 2019, by the foundation's pages.

The name: Público and a Brazilian account give the cession of the Pêra-Manca name in 1987 by José António de Oliveira Soares, the heir of Casa Soares, on the condition that it mark the foundation's exceptional wine; Casa Soares ceased after phylloxera; the first Pêra-Manca of the new era the 1990 harvest, made since only in years judged exceptional. Borne out; the record keeps the late 1980s for the author's 1989.

The making, the house blocked where merchants could answer: Aragonez and Trincadeira (one merchant 55 and 45), fermentation in French oak balseiros at a controlled temperature with a long maceration after it, eighteen months in French oak tonéis and four years (48 months) in bottle in the monastery's cellars, on four merchants (Sommelier Vinhos, Garrafeira Imperial, Garrafeira Pepe, Vinhos 14 Regiões). Borne out; the casks of 3,000 litres stand on the house's sheet alone.

The Cartuxa Reserva: first made in 1987 on the house's 2019 sheet and Creative Gourmet; Alicante Bouschet, Aragonez and Cabernet Sauvignon on the 2019 sheet, Alicante Bouschet and Aragonez alone on the 2017 sheet and a merchant; fifteen months in new French oak and 48 in bottle for the 2019.

The questions: one right answer each, options of one kind (four pairs of grapes, four ways a name was got); the house rules: nobody living named (the heir of 1987 and the winemaking team met, not named), no price (a merchant's price met), no score, no production (a bottle count met and not used), no judging superlative, British, no dash.

changed.was: The name is older than the wine. In the nineteenth century a farming house of Évora made a wine called Pêra-Manca, and Portuguese writers like to tell, as legend, that the navigator who reached Brazil in 1500 carried a wine of that name in his ships. The farming house later ceased trading. The Fundação Eugénio de Almeida was set up on 25 September 1963, endowed by an engineer of that family as a private charitable foundation, and its wines are made at the Cartuxa winery, named for the Carthusian monks of the monastery of Santa Maria Scala Coeli outside the city; the first Cartuxa Reserva came in 1987. In the late 1980s an heir of the old farming house offered the Pêra-Manca name to the foundation, on the condition, as the press tells it, that it be kept for the exceptional wine made there. The first Pêra-Manca of the foundation followed in 1990, and the red has since been bottled only in the years the house judges worthy, after eighteen months in large casks and years in the monastery's cellars. For a sommelier, Pêra-Manca is the Alentejo's red of occasion, and its vintages are read one by one.

changed.was: Herdade do Esporão is far older than its wine. By the house's account its bounds were fixed in 1267, when it was the Defesa do Esporão, and have hardly moved since; the Reconquista had taken Monsaraz and Reguengos in 1232. Its tower, raised in the fifteenth century by a holder of the entailed estate, stands on the estate, and the Counts of Alcáçovas held the land until 1973. That year two partners bought it, founding the company that carries its name. After the revolution of April 1974 the estate was occupied in the land reform, and only in 1985 did it give the harvest of its first wine, Esporão Reserva red. With that wine came a custom: each year an invited artist, almost always Portuguese, makes the work that fills its label, a painting on the first of them. A winery was built in 1987, the wines went abroad from 1989, and in 2000 came a second winery, the Adega dos Lagares, and the first Private Selection red. For a sommelier, Esporão Reserva is the Alentejo's own grapes blended with Cabernet Sauvignon, under a label that has been a gallery since 1985.

changed.was: Adega de Borba is a co-operative. Its first board took office on 30 April 1955, and by its own account it was the first of a series of co-operative wineries set up across the Alentejo with the support of the Junta Nacional do Vinho, the national wine board of the time. The growers of Borba brought their grapes to one shared cellar. In 1964 the co-operative made the first vintage of its Reserva red and dressed it in a label made of cork, in homage, as the house tells it, to the Alentejo's other harvest, the bark of its cork oaks. The wine became known by its label: the house's own pages call its Reserva the Rótulo de Cortiça, the cork label. It has been made since only in the years the co-operative judges exceptional, so that the vintage of 2018 was only the twenty fifth edition of the wine. For a sommelier, the cork label teaches two things: that a co-operative's red can be made to keep for a decade, and that a label can become a wine's name.

tested: The founding and the Syrah, the author's sources blocked: 1988 for the couple's start on Portugal Wine Expert and Wine and Earth, the Danish and American couple arriving by sailing boat, the vines of 1991, the first Incógnito of 1998, so named because Syrah was not allowed; one account has the first wine labelled only as a table wine, another the grape spelt in an acrostic on the back label.
The year Syrah was admitted: 2002 by two accounts, the late 1990s by one and a year after the first Incógnito by another; unsettled, so the record keeps later.

The making, on the house's sheets: the 2021 with half whole bunches, two and a half weeks on the skins and six months in used 500 litre barrels; the 2023 with a quarter whole bunches, two weeks, twelve months in used 500 litre oak and eight in steel, 12.5 per cent alcohol, on sandy, silty limestone; the first Incógnito of biodynamic vines. The older reviews (Wine Enthusiast) found the wine powerful, so the glass, ageing and serving are told by vintage.

The questions: one right answer each, options of one kind (four categories, four rules); the house rules: nobody living named (the founders and their daughter not named), no price, no score, nothing volatile (recent vintages refused by the lint and dated instead), no judging superlative, British, no dash.

changed.why: The 2023 sheet gives a quarter whole bunches, two weeks and twelve months in used 500 litre oak against the 2021's half, two and a half weeks and six months.

swapNote: The author proposed no swap, and the refuter proposes none. The five picks stand: each is a real house of the Alentejo with the wine it is known by (Mouchão, Pêra-Manca Tinto, Esporão Reserva red, Adega de Borba Reserva with its cork label, Incógnito). Nothing read rules any of them out.
planNotes: mouchao: answered. No member of the family is named, no two sources giving any one's dates; no year without a Mouchão red was found (the library's accepted years is not borne out, while Tonel 3 and 4 is made only in years of full ripeness by the house); Tonel 3 and 4 is in others. The why's Alicante Bouschet planted since the nineteenth century is the grape's coming, not the vines of the flagship, which grow in a vineyard of 1988.

cartuxa: answered. The founder is now named with his dates from two sources; the red's first vintage of 1990 is borne out by Público and a second account; the older story is told as legend; the Cartuxa Reserva is in others.

esporao: answered. 1973 and the first Reserva of 1985 are borne out by independent accounts; the grapes are in words and by vintage; the founding partners and the founder's son are living and never named; the white Reserva is in others. The why's winery of the 1980s that led the revival is not said in the record.

adega-de-borba: answered. 1955 and the cork label of 1964 are borne out by two independent accounts; the grapes are the house's four. The why's taught a generation is unsourced (the author found the same) and is not in the record; the marble country is not said in the record either.

cortes-de-cima: answered in part. 1998 is borne out; the year of the rule change is not settled (2002 by two accounts, the late 1990s by one, a year after the first Incógnito by another); the founders are never named; the label is Vinho Regional Alentejano, while one account says the first vintage could only be a table wine.
